# Episode 1 — script M1b (generated from script.tpl.md and out/claims.json; do not edit)

## cold-open

- `co-maya` Maya locked in 7.62%.
- `co-today` This week's average: 7.03%.
- `co-cost` Refinancing costs $5,124.
- `co-question` So when does that money come back?

## act1

- `a1-lab` This is a lab for money decisions: we run the numbers on public data, and show every assumption.
- `a1-scope` US only. The rates here are history, not a forecast.
- `a1-rehook` By the end, you will see the exact rate drop that pays back a refinance like Maya's within 36 months, and how every rate drop since 1971 actually played out.
- `a1-maya` She borrowed $375,000 in October 2023, the month the 30-year rate peaked.
- `a1-you` And if your own rate starts with a 7, the question is yours as well.
- `a1-q` First: is Maya's bill unusual?
- `a1-median` No. In 2025, the median closing cost on a rate-and-term refinance was $5,124.
- `a1-hmda` Lenders must report every mortgage they make, and since 2018, the total loan costs of each one.
- `a1-count` That is the middle of 488,241 such loans that lenders reported under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act.
- `a1-spread` Half of those borrowers paid between $3,443 and $8,270.
- `a1-terms` The bill is the closing costs: origination charges, discount points, the appraisal, title insurance, and the rest.
- `a1-turn` But that bill barely grows with the loan, so it lands much harder on some borrowers than on others.
- `a1-dan` Take Dan, who borrowed $115,000 in the same month, at the same rate.
- `a1-dan2` On loans under $150,000, the median bill was 3.4% of the amount borrowed.
- `a1-dan3` For Dan, that is $3,667: fewer dollars than Maya, but a far larger share of his loan.
- `a1-priya` Priya borrowed $1,005,000.
- `a1-priya2` On loans of $750,000 and more, the bill was 0.5%.
- `a1-priya3` For Priya, that is $5,034: about Maya's bill, on a loan nearly three times the size.
- `a1-save` What the bill buys is a lower payment. At today's rate, Maya's payment falls by $221 a month.
- `a1-rule` Divide the bill by that saving, and you get the answer most calculators give: 24 months.
- `a1-payoff` By that count, the refinance has paid for itself. Or has it?

## act2

- `a2-q` Here is what that division leaves out.
- `a2-old` Maya's old loan already has 35 payments behind it.
- `a2-reset` A refinance starts a fresh 30 years, so the new loan pays the balance down more slowly than the old one would have.
- `a2-why` Early payments are mostly interest. Maya's old loan was just starting to pay down real principal, and the new one starts that schedule over.
- `a2-owe` So count what she still owes on each loan, month by month.
- `a2-gap` After 24 months, the new loan leaves her owing $1,133 more than the old one would have.
- `a2-real` So, counting what she still owes, break-even is not 24 months. It is 30.
- `a2-thesis` Most calculators stop at the monthly saving. The balance keeps the score for longer.
- `a2-small` The smaller the cut, the bigger that gap.
- `a2-s025` At a cut of 0.25 points, the division would promise 38 months.
- `a2-s025b` Counting the balance, Maya never catches up before her old loan would have been paid off.
- `a2-cliff` Below 0.5 points, the fresh start can swallow the savings entirely.
- `a2-s10` At a cut of 1 point, the two answers nearly meet.
- `a2-s10b` The division says 16 months; the balance says 18.
- `a2-dan` Now Dan. At today's rate, his payment falls by only $68 a month.
- `a2-dan2` The division says 55 months. Counting what he still owes, it is 75.
- `a2-dan3` If Dan sells after 3 years, the refinance leaves him $1,777 behind.
- `a2-dan4` After 7 years, he is only $386 ahead.
- `a2-priya` Priya saves $593 a month, and is even after 11 months.
- `a2-priya2` If she sells after 3 years, she is $11,482 ahead; after 7, $30,387.
- `a2-maya` And Maya, the middle case: $1,039 ahead after 3 years, $8,093 after 7.
- `a2-sell` Put another way: a house sold before the break-even month turns the refinance into a loss, and one kept past it turns it into a gain.
- `a2-payoff` Same rate, same month. The answer depends on the size of the loan, how old it is, and how long the house is kept.

## act3

- `a3-q` The division also assumes today's rate is the last one. What happened in the real drops?
- `a3-all` We found every fall of at least 1 point in the 30-year rate since 1971: 13 of them.
- `a3-rules` In each, someone like Maya borrows at the peak and refinances in the first month the rate is 1 point lower.
- `a3-costs` Closing costs use each year's median share; before 2018, lenders did not report them, so a fixed share is used and marked illustrative.
- `a3-range` Counting what was still owed, break-even took between 10 and 20 months.
- `a3-simple` The simple division would have said between 10 and 21.
- `a3-young` Nearly the same, because those loans were only months old when the rate fell, so the fresh start cost them little. Maya's loan is 35 payments old.
- `a3-81` The biggest fall began after the peak of 18.63% in 1981.
- `a3-81b` A refinance 2 months later paid back in 13 months, and the rate kept falling.
- `a3-priya` For Priya's loan size, every one of those drops paid back within 6 months.
- `a3-dan` For a loan like Dan's, with the bill a bigger share, the same drops took between 18 and 39 months.
- `a3-turn` But in 3 of those drops, the rate fell another 1 point before the first refinance had paid for itself.
- `a3-twice` Those borrowers met the same question twice, and a second refinance starts a new clock with a new bill.
- `a3-example` In the drop that began in July 1984, the refinance came in November 1984.
- `a3-example2` It needed 19 months to pay back, and the next drop of 1 point came 7 months later.
- `a3-quiet` In the other 10, the first refinance was the one that mattered.
- `a3-23` Maya's own drop began in October 2023. A cut of 1 point first arrived in August 2024.
- `a3-23be` Refinancing then would have paid back in 19 months.
- `a3-answer` So, how far do rates have to fall before a refinance pays for itself?
- `a3-answer2` For a loan like Maya's, counting what is still owed, a cut of 0.5 points pays it back within 36 months.
- `a3-answer3` Dan would need 1.12 points. Priya, 0.2.
- `a3-today` Today's cut is 0.59 points. For Maya, that means ahead after 30 months, and behind if the house is sold before then.
- `a3-limit` That answer has limits. It leaves out taxes and any return on the cash, and it assumes the bill is paid up front, not added to the loan.
- `a3-median` It uses medians: half of borrowers paid more than $5,124, and an offered rate can differ from the survey average.
- `a3-history` And it is history, not a forecast: nothing here says where rates go next.
- `a3-close` What history does show is the shape of the trade: a known bill up front, against savings and a balance that settle month by month.

## method

- `m-rates` Method. Rates are Freddie Mac's weekly survey via FRED, checked against the Optimal Blue index since 2017.
- `m-drops` A drop counts when the monthly average falls at least 1 point from a peak before rising 1 point from its low.
- `m-costs` Costs are HMDA loan-level data from 2018 to 2025: originated refinances, first lien, 30-year term.
- `m-chars` Maya, Dan and Priya are illustrative: each one's loan and bill are the medians for that loan size.
- `m-assume` Break-even counts payment savings plus the difference in balance still owed. Closing costs paid in cash; no taxes. Every figure is listed in the description.

## outro

- `o-recap` A small cut needs a long stay. A small loan needs a bigger cut. And a young loan loses less to the fresh start.
- `o-you` If the rate on your own statement starts with a 7, the same three questions apply: how big the cut, how old the loan, and how long the stay.
- `o-close` The monthly saving is only half of the answer. The other half, just as real, is what is still owed.
- `o-sources` The sources are linked in the description, and the next decision is already on the bench.
